title: Daily Active Users
description:
For each calendar day on which anything happened, report how many distinct users were active.

Name the columns `day` and `active_users`. Return the result in any order.
hint: DATE() strips the time part off a timestamp. Count DISTINCT users, not rows.

title: Users Who Never Did Anything
description:
Report the `name` of every registered user with no events at all.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
hint: NOT EXISTS is immune to the NULL trap that breaks NOT IN.

title: First And Last Activity
description:
For every user who has at least one event, report the timestamp of their earliest and latest event.

Name the columns `name`, `first_seen` and `last_seen`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT u.name, MIN(e.event_time) AS first_seen, MAX(e.event_time) AS last_seen
FROM users u
JOIN events e ON e.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.id, u.name;
hint: ISO timestamps sort correctly as text, so MIN and MAX work directly on them.

title: Pivot Events Into Columns
description:
For every user with events, report how many logins, views and purchases they have — one row per user, three columns.

Name the columns `name`, `logins`, `views` and `purchases`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT u.name,
       SUM(CASE WHEN e.event_type = 'login' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS logins,
       SUM(CASE WHEN e.event_type = 'view' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS views,
       SUM(CASE WHEN e.event_type = 'purchase' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS purchases
FROM users u
JOIN events e ON e.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.id, u.name;
hint: SQL has no PIVOT here — conditional aggregation with CASE inside SUM does the same job.

title: Minutes Since Your Last Event
description:
For every event report how many minutes passed since that user's previous event, rounded to 2 decimals. A user's first event reports NULL.

Name the columns `id`, `user_id` and `minutes_since_prev`. Return the result in any order.
hint: JULIANDAY returns days as a float — multiply the difference by 24*60 for minutes.

title: Bought On Day One
description:
Report the name of every user who made a purchase on the same calendar day as their very first event.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT DISTINCT u.name
FROM users u
JOIN events e ON e.user_id = u.id
WHERE e.event_type = 'purchase'
  AND DATE(e.event_time) = (SELECT DATE(MIN(event_time)) FROM events x WHERE x.user_id = u.id);
hint: A correlated subquery finds each user's own first event date; compare the purchase's date against it.

title: Each User's Most Frequent Event
description:
For every user report the event type they perform most often, together with the count. If a user ties across several types, report all of the tied types. Ignore events with a NULL type.

Name the columns `name`, `event_type` and `times`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
WITH counts AS (
  SELECT u.name, e.event_type, COUNT(*) AS times,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY u.id ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS rnk
  FROM users u
  JOIN events e ON e.user_id = u.id
  WHERE e.event_type IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY u.id, u.name, e.event_type
)
SELECT name, event_type, times FROM counts WHERE rnk = 1;
hint: A window function may sit on top of a GROUP BY — RANK() OVER (... ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) ranks the groups themselves.

title: Longest Daily Streak
description:
For every user with at least one event, report the length of their longest run of **consecutive calendar days** with activity. A single active day counts as a streak of 1.

Name the columns `name` and `longest_streak`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE(event_time) AS d FROM events
),
grouped AS (
  SELECT user_id, d,
         DATE(d, '-' || ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY d) || ' day') AS grp
  FROM days
),
runs AS (
  SELECT user_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS len
  FROM grouped
  GROUP BY user_id, grp
)
SELECT u.name, MAX(r.len) AS longest_streak
FROM runs r
JOIN users u ON u.id = r.user_id
GROUP BY u.id, u.name;
hint: The gaps-and-islands trick: subtract a row number (in days) from each date. Consecutive dates all collapse to the same anchor date, which becomes the group key.

title: Active Three Days Running
description:
Report the name of every user who was active on **three or more consecutive calendar days** at some point.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE(event_time) AS d FROM events
),
grouped AS (
  SELECT user_id, DATE(d, '-' || ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY d) || ' day') AS grp
  FROM days
)
SELECT DISTINCT u.name
FROM grouped g
JOIN users u ON u.id = g.user_id
GROUP BY g.user_id, g.grp, u.name
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
hint: Same islands trick as the longest streak, but you only need HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 — and DISTINCT in case a user has several qualifying runs.

title: Count Sessions With A 30-Minute Timeout
description:
A user's session ends after 30 minutes of inactivity: an event starts a new session if it is their first, or if more than 30 minutes passed since their previous event.

Report how many sessions each user with events had.

Name the columns `name` and `sessions`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
WITH gaps AS (
  SELECT user_id,
         CASE WHEN LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time, id) IS NULL
                OR (JULIANDAY(event_time) - JULIANDAY(LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time, id))) * 24 * 60 > 30
              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new
  FROM events
)
SELECT u.name, SUM(g.is_new) AS sessions
FROM gaps g
JOIN users u ON u.id = g.user_id
GROUP BY u.id, u.name;
hint: Flag each event as starting a session or not, then simply add the flags up.

title: Came Back The Next Day
description:
Report the name of every user who was active again on the calendar day **immediately after** their first active day.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT user_id, DATE(MIN(event_time)) AS first_day FROM events GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT DISTINCT u.name
FROM firsts f
JOIN events e ON e.user_id = f.user_id AND DATE(e.event_time) = DATE(f.first_day, '+1 day')
JOIN users u ON u.id = f.user_id;
hint: Compute each user's first day, then look for any event exactly one day later with DATE(d, '+1 day').

title: Rolling Seven-Day Activity
description:
For each day with activity, report the number of events that occurred within the seven-day window ending on that day (the day itself plus the six calendar days before it).

Name the columns `day` and `events_7d`. Return the result in any order.
hint: A ROWS frame counts rows present in the data; a RANGE frame over JULIANDAY counts actual calendar distance — which is what "seven days" means.

title: Longest Absence
description:
For every user with two or more events, report the longest gap in whole days between two of their consecutive events, rounded to 2 decimals.

Name the columns `name` and `longest_gap_days`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
WITH gaps AS (
  SELECT user_id,
         JULIANDAY(event_time) - JULIANDAY(LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time, id)) AS gap
  FROM events
)
SELECT u.name, ROUND(MAX(g.gap), 2) AS longest_gap_days
FROM gaps g
JOIN users u ON u.id = g.user_id
WHERE g.gap IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY u.id, u.name;
hint: Filtering out the NULL gap (each user's first event) also removes single-event users automatically.

title: Viewed Then Bought
description:
Report the name of every user who made a purchase **strictly after** one of their own view events.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT DISTINCT u.name
FROM events v
JOIN events p
  ON p.user_id = v.user_id
 AND p.event_type = 'purchase'
 AND p.event_time > v.event_time
JOIN users u ON u.id = v.user_id
WHERE v.event_type = 'view';
hint: Self-join the events table to itself on the same user, with a time ordering between the two rows.

title: Started With A Purchase
description:
Report the name of every user whose very first event (earliest timestamp, ties broken by the smaller event `id`) was a purchase.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT user_id, event_type,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time, id) AS rn
  FROM events
)
SELECT u.name
FROM ordered o
JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE o.rn = 1 AND o.event_type = 'purchase';
hint: When timestamps tie, the ORDER BY inside ROW_NUMBER needs a tie-breaker or the answer is not deterministic.

title: Busiest Hour Of The Day
description:
Report the hour of day (as a two-digit string, `00` to `23`) with the most events overall, along with the count. Report every hour if there is a tie.

Name the columns `hour` and `events`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
WITH per_hour AS (
  SELECT strftime('%H', event_time) AS hour, COUNT(*) AS events
  FROM events
  GROUP BY hour
)
SELECT hour, events
FROM per_hour
WHERE events = (SELECT MAX(events) FROM per_hour);
hint: strftime('%H', ...) keeps the leading zero because it returns text. Compare against MAX so ties survive.

title: Median Events Per User
description:
Considering only users who have at least one event, report the median number of events per user.

Name the column `median_events`. The result is exactly one row.
hint: Same median recipe as before, applied to per-user counts rather than raw values.
